t: for they are forbidden all work of labor except work for the sake of eating. Unlike Shabbat and Yom Kippur, on which even work for the sake of eating is forbidden.
with witnesses and warning. Witnesses to the act of transgression who testify to it before a court, and a warning before the act of transgression (Hilchot Sanhedrin 12:1-2).

there is division of labors on Shabbat, but there is no division of labors on a festival. If he did several different primary labors on Shabbat, he is punished for each of them separately (Hilchot Shabbat 7:7), but on a festival he receives one punishment for all the labors he did.
every labor for which one is liable on Shabbat. For the list of labors forbidden on Shabbat see Hilchot Shabbat 7:1.

since carrying out was permitted on a festival for the sake of eating, it was permitted even not for the sake of eating. Likewise, since kindling was permitted for need, it was permitted even not for need (Commentary to the Mishnah, Beitzah 1:5, and see Maggid Mishneh).
and he may carry back and forth whatever he wishes and complete his needs. See below 5:1-8 for certain restrictions on carrying on a festival.

but other labors that could be done from the day before... may not be done on a festival. And kindling that is permitted not for the sake of eating is permitted only when one kindles from an existing flame, but it is forbidden to create fire on a festival because he could do so before the festival (see below 4:1).
and one does not thresh, etc.. The actions that make up the process of producing flour from wheat (for an explanation of these actions see the Biur on Hilchot Shabbat 7:1).
grinding spices and the like. Although they are not eaten by themselves, they are used to prepare food (for the details of these laws see below 3:12-13).
what he will eat on a weekday. What he wants to prepare for the needs of a weekday.
and left over. Left a portion of the food.
baker. A baker or cook.
to a small jug. A small vessel for water.
provided he does not act cunningly. That he not act as if cooking for guests or the like, when his intention is really to cook for the needs of tomorrow.

even on a Shabbat after a festival, etc.. Although if he transgressed deliberately and cooked on the festival for the sake of Shabbat they permitted him to eat it on Shabbat, in the case of one who acts cunningly they were stricter, so that people not come to do this regularly (see below 6:10 and the rulings and opinions there).
endangered. That there is concern it will die soon, and he wants to slaughter it before it dies and becomes a carcass.

it alone may be done for you. "Only what every person is to eat, that alone may be done for you," and from this they derived that the permission to do labors for food on a festival is only "for you" and not for others.
we invite the gentile on Shabbat. Invite him to a meal (see also Hilchot Shabbat 6:21).
he will increase. Prepare more food in a forbidden manner.
because he can divide the dough. Therefore they did not permit baking the gentile's half.
troops. Non-Jewish soldiers who arrive at inhabited places and the locals must provide them with services such as preparing bread.
if when giving bread to a child they are not particular. That they give the child some of the bread baked from the soldiers' flour, and the soldiers are not particular about it.
dogs' dough. Dough kneaded with coarse wheat components and intended mainly for animals (Commentary to the Mishnah, Challah 1:8).
for if guests had come to him, that dish would have been fit for them. Therefore there is no absolute transgression here and one is not flogged for it.
because of the decree of the bathhouse. The Sages restricted bathing on Shabbat and festivals because the bath attendants would heat the water on Shabbat (see Hilchot Shabbat 22:2).
for they decreed this matter only on Shabbat alone. The Sages forbade washing one's whole body in hot water heated the day before only on Shabbat, and not on a festival.
whether because it resembles a labor or leads to a labor. And it was therefore forbidden by the Sages (see Hilchot Shabbat 21:1).
whether because of a shevut. Actions forbidden so that a person's affairs and speech on Shabbat will differ from those of a weekday (see ibid. 24:1).
or things that are permitted on a festival. Such as carrying out (see Commentary to the Mishnah, Beitzah 5:2).
and whatever is forbidden to move on Shabbat. See Hilchot Shabbat 24:12-13, and chapters 25-26.
except for the sake of eating and the like. For the sake of food they permitted moving these objects.

the prohibition of muktzeh. The prohibition of eating on a festival something that was set aside from eating and that one decided not to eat (Commentary to the Mishnah, Beitzah 1:1), and also the prohibition of using things that were not designated for use on the eve of the festival (see below 2:11 ff.). Muktzeh that is forbidden for eating and for use is also forbidden to move (see below halakhah 20, 2:17).
and dovecote pigeons. They are not considered prepared (see below 2:5).

but on Shabbat everything is prepared for Shabbat and needs no preparation. On Shabbat anything fit for food is permitted even if it was not designated for eating, such as fruits kept for trade (see Hilchot Shabbat 26:14).

the newly born. Something that came into being on the festival that one had not considered beforehand, such as fruit that fell from the tree (Commentary to the Mishnah, Beitzah 1:1; and see below 2:11-12, 2:18).

a weekday prepares for Shabbat, etc.. Something that came into being on a weekday is permitted to eat the next day on Shabbat or a festival, but if it came into being on a festival that falls on the eve of Shabbat, or on a Shabbat that falls on the eve of a festival, it is forbidden the next day.

and even though the hen is designated for eating, etc.. And it itself is prepared and permitted on the festival, nevertheless the egg is forbidden, since laying the egg takes place on the day after the completion of its formation, and since it was laid on the festival, it turns out that its formation was completed on Shabbat and the hen prepared the egg for the festival.
and they forbade it on every festival. Even if it falls after a weekday, in which case a weekday would have prepared for the festival.
in a thousand. Eggs.

and anything that has a means of permitting it. A forbidden item that has a way to be permitted or whose time of prohibition is limited; the Sages forbade it even if it was mixed with a thousand and is not nullified by a majority (see Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot 15:10).
complete. Ready.
chance. An accident.

that we in the Diaspora observe each of these two festival days is a custom. At the time when the month was sanctified on the basis of sighting and the Diaspora did not know when the festival fell, they kept it for two days out of doubt. Even now, when the festival is set by calculation of the calendar and there is no longer any doubt, the Sages instituted continuing the custom they had practiced before, of observing two days (see below 6:14, Hilchot Kiddush ha-Chodesh 5:4-5).
and the second festival day is by rabbinic enactment. The authority of the second day is not from the Torah but from the words of the Sages (see Hilchot Kiddush ha-Chodesh, ibid., halakhah 6).
and among the things newly instituted in exile. The whole matter of the second festival day belongs to the Diaspora, and in the Land of Israel one observes one day, except on Rosh Hashanah.
and in Hilchot Kiddush ha-Chodesh of this book. 5:4-12.
the origin of this custom. The root of the custom of the second festival day in the Diaspora.
and for what reason they observe Rosh Hashanah for two days everywhere. Even in the Land of Israel (see ibid. 5:7-8).
even though it is by rabbinic enactment. And it is not like the first day, whose obligation is from the Torah.
and even that of Rosh Hashanah. Although its two days are considered one holiness (below halakhah 24), nevertheless on the second day he is not flogged by Torah law, but only with rabbinic lashes.
outside the boundary. Two thousand cubits from the place where he rests (see Hilchot Shabbat 27:1).
rabbinic lashes. Lashes by rabbinic law.
we place under a ban. They impose a ban (niddui) on him (see also Hilchot Talmud Torah 6:14; for the laws of the ban see ibid. 7:2 ff.).
if he is not one of the disciples. For if he was a Torah scholar, they try as far as possible to avoid placing him under a ban (see ibid. 7:1).
forbidden for eulogy and fasting. It is forbidden to eulogize the dead on it or to fix a fast on it (see Hilchot Ta'aniyot 1:6, 1:9, Hilchot Evel 11:3).
and obligated in rejoicing. The rejoicing of the festival (see below 6:17-18).
should attend to. Should take care of.
and they do for him all his needs, etc.. See Hilchot Evel 4:1.

even on the two festival days of Rosh Hashanah. Although they were treated strictly, as one long day (below halakhah 24), they were nevertheless lenient on the second day regarding burial of the dead.
they are two holinesses and not like one day. The Sages did not consider them one long day but two separate days.

therefore something that was muktzeh on the first festival day... if he prepared it for the second, it is permitted. Unlike a festival and Shabbat adjacent to each other, which do not prepare for one another (above halakhah 19), in two festival days the first prepares for the second.
it is permitted to apply eye-paint on the second festival day even though there is no illness. It is permitted to put a substance on the eye even for no medical need.

they are one holiness and are considered as one day. Unlike the other festivals of the Diaspora, the two days of Rosh Hashanah are considered one long day, and therefore what was muktzeh or newly born on the first is forbidden on the second, since the second day is a continuation of the first and there is no preparation from the first for the second.
but only regarding the dead. That its law is that it is buried by Jews even on the second day of Rosh Hashanah.
a Shabbat adjacent to a festival. Before it or after it, and the egg was laid on the first of the two days.

forbidden on the second. Since the egg was forbidden on the first day because of the prohibition of nolad, it is also forbidden on the second, for Shabbat and a festival do not prepare for one another (see above halakhah 19).
even if it was laid on the second festival day. Which is only rabbinic; nevertheless its law is that of a festival, and an egg laid on it is forbidden on the Shabbat that follows.
a chick born on a festival. That hatched from the egg.
because it is muktzeh. For on the eve of the festival, while it was in the egg, it was not ready for eating.

if its mother was designated for eating it is permitted. But if its mother was designated for work or the like she was forbidden (above 1:19), and the calf was also forbidden. That which is in her womb is permitted. For a fetus found in the womb of an animal that was slaughtered may be eaten without slaughter (Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot 5:14).

these are prepared. Even though during the day he cannot take and slaughter them, since they are outside the two-thousand-cubit boundary of the city (see Hilchot Shabbat 27:1), because they are accustomed to return every evening to lodge within the boundary they are prepared, and even if they came in the middle of the day he may slaughter them.

a consecrated animal that developed a blemish, etc.. Such as a firstborn or animal tithe, which when they have a blemish are not offered in the Temple and are permitted to be eaten after ordinary slaughter (Hilchot Bekhorot 1:2-3, 6:4). Therefore if on the eve of the festival they had no blemish, they are muktzeh because he had not considered them.

therefore it is forbidden to examine the blemishes of consecrated animals on a festival, as a decree lest the sage permit it, etc.. In general one may not slaughter a firstborn that has a blemish before showing it to a sage who is expert in examining blemishes (see ibid. 3:1-2). The Sages decreed that the sage may not examine blemishes on a festival even if they arose before the festival, lest he permit a blemish that arose on the festival itself and they come to slaughter on the festival.

but he may see the blemish on the eve of the festival and permit it the next day. On the eve of the festival he examines the blemish to see whether it is a blemish for which the firstborn is slaughtered, and on the festival he investigates the circumstances in which the blemish arose (and see Hilchot Bekhorot 2:7 ff.), and rules whether it may be slaughtered (based on Babylonian Talmud, Beitzah 27a-b).
a firstborn that was born with its blemish. An animal that gave birth on a festival to a firstborn offspring, which was born already blemished.

it is prepared. Since before it was born it was prepared along with its mother (when she is designated for eating, as above halakhah 1), and when it was born it was already blemished and fit to be slaughtered and eaten, so its law is that of an unconsecrated animal born on a festival.
and one does not examine it on a festival. But its blemish is not examined to permit it for slaughter, just as one does not examine a consecrated animal that developed a blemish on a festival.
provides for him in his place. Lowers to him in the pit his essential needs, such as food and drink.

it and its offspring. An animal and its young, which it is forbidden to slaughter both on one day (see Hilchot Shechitah 12:1), and therefore he cannot raise them in order to slaughter both on a festival.
examination. Examination of the body to make sure it was not injured in a way that defines it as a treifah (see ibid. 9:9, 9:17).

it is possible that it will be found valid and eaten. It may be that nothing will be found in it that defines it as a treifah and it will be permitted for eating, and therefore it is permitted to slaughter it.
upper room. A floor above the ground floor.
in the nesting jars. Earthenware vessels fixed in the walls and meant for birds to nest in.
in the birah. In a structure outside the area of the house.
from the evening. Close to the entrance of the festival.
and he need not shake. Those he designated; it is enough to designate them by speaking. [Note: Maimonides vocalizes the word "chickens" in the Commentary to the Mishnah as tarnegelin.]
black and white. Black and white chicks.
and found black ones in place of white ones, etc.. In the place where the white chicks had been before, he now found black ones, or the reverse.
and any doubt about being prepared is forbidden. Even in a case of doubt whether it was prepared from the eve of the festival or not, it is forbidden.

if he designated two and found three, all are forbidden. For if the third is in addition to the two he designated, muktzeh has become mixed with the prepared, and such a mixture is forbidden. And if those he designated were all replaced by the three he found, then none of them is prepared and all are forbidden (Commentary to the Mishnah, Beitzah 1:4, based on the Gemara).
three and found two, they are permitted. Since it is reasonable that these are the ones he designated, and one of them flew off.
to fly. To fly on their own.
around a corner. Beyond a corner.
within fifty cubits. At such a distance there is concern that the young bird walked from the other nest (see Hilchot Gezelah va-Avedah 15:18).
one that hops. A bird that does not fly but hops on its feet.
level. In a straight line from its own nest.
in vivaria. Enclosed places for raising animals.
anything that still requires hunting, until one says, Bring a trap and we will catch it. For to take it from the vivarium, a hunting device is needed.
it is muktzeh. Since it is not within reach without hunting, it is not defined as prepared.
that nested. Raised young.
because his mind is on them. Because from the eve of the festival he intended to take from them on the festival if he needed.
traps. Hunting devices such as a net.
he may not take from them on a festival. From the animals caught in a trap.
unless he knows that they were caught from the eve of the festival. For a doubt about being prepared is forbidden (above halakhah 6).
one who dams a water channel. Blocks a channel of water.

that were already caught from the eve of the festival. Some explain that he blocked the channel from the eve of the festival at both its ends, so the fish inside could not leave, and thereby they were already caught from the eve of the festival (Maggid Mishneh, and see R. Y. Kafih); and some explain that he dammed the channel at one side, and although the fish had not yet reached the dam on the eve of the festival, since it is clear that in time the fish would gather at the dam and not be able to escape (because of the flow of the water and the like), they are considered already caught from the eve of the festival (Yad Peshutah).
and it was breached. Broken through.

he takes from the place of the breach. And they are not considered muktzeh, since they were prepared for eating on the eve of the festival, and the prevention from taking them was not because of themselves but because of the prohibition of making a breach in a house (Maggid Mishneh, based on Ramban).
one who stands on the drying ground. A place designated for drying fruit, and these fruits are not yet designated for eating, and he wants to designate for the festival fruit that is there.

in the Sabbatical year. In a Sabbatical year there is no obligation to separate tithes, so these fruits are not lacking tithes, and what prevents eating them on the festival is only the lack of preparation.
that he mark. That he mark the place that he is designating for the festival.
gift. A present.
these are forbidden until the evening. Until the end of the festival, out of concern that the gentile plucked or caught them on the festival.

and he waits long enough for them to be done. At the end of the festival they are not permitted immediately but only after the time needed to do the forbidden act has passed, so that the Jew gains no benefit from the work having been done for him on Shabbat (see Hilchot Shabbat 6:2, 6:8).
and what is brought for one Jew from outside the boundary is permitted to another Jew. What a gentile brings from outside the boundary for a Jew is forbidden only to the one for whom it was brought.
to heat with them. To use them for kindling.
newly born. They came into being on the festival, as above 1:18.
into the oven. In their time there were ovens with an opening at the top.
he adds to them prepared wood. Adds to them wood that is not muktzeh.
and storehouse. A depot.

one does not begin, etc.. If they had not already taken from them before the festival, one does not take from them for the first time unless they were designated for heating from the eve of the festival.
and if the straw was mixed with thorns. So that it is not fit for animal food but only for burning, it is designated for heating and needs no preparation.
one does not split wood. One does not cut logs for heating.
from a stack of beams. A pile of beams.
but one may heat with whole vessels. Because they are permitted for use and for moving.
similarly. Like vessels, which if they broke from the eve of the festival are permitted, and if not they are forbidden.
one may heat with their shells on a festival. Because the shells were designated for heating from the eve of the festival, and so they are not muktzeh.
one may not heat with their shells. Because they are nolad.
and there are versions. In the Gemara.

those adjacent to the walls of a sukkah. Wood that is not part of the wall, so there is no issue of dismantling a tent or of muktzeh; but from the wood of the sukkah itself it is forbidden to take on a festival because one violates dismantling a tent (see Hilchot Shabbat 10:15), and on Sukkot there is also a muktzeh prohibition on the wood of the sukkah (see Hilchot Sukkah 6:15).
but one does not bring wood from the field, even if it was gathered there from the evening. For since it remained in the field it is not considered prepared.
but he gathers in the field in front of him. He makes a pile of grass and small pieces of wood he finds around him, for what is in front of him is considered prepared.
enclosed, not for the sake of dwelling. Surrounded by a partition and not meant for living in (and see Hilchot Shabbat, chapter 16).
provided that it has an opening and is within the Shabbat boundary. For if not, the place is considered an open field.
opening. A lock.
in a karpef. An area surrounded by a partition and meant for various uses.
if it was endangered. If there was concern that it would die soon.
he cuts it up for the dogs. He may feed it to the dogs.

a consecrated animal that died and terumah that became impure may not be moved from their place. For they cannot be used, since their law is to be burned, and the Sages forbade burning them on a festival (see below 3:8-9).
to take from them. From those animals.
if he designated for himself a corner of his courtyard. If he placed it in a certain corner so that he could take from it when needed.
ashes that were burned from the eve of the festival. That were already ashes on the eve of the festival.
it is permitted to move it, for it is still fire. Since it is fit for roasting an egg, it is defined as fire and may be used like fire.
a pick. A tool for digging the ground.
and loosened it. Removed it from its place.
crumbles. Pulverizes.
covers with it. The blood of slaughter (see below 3:1).
he may not pound it on a festival. Because of the prohibition of grinding on a festival.
prepared earth or ashes that may be moved. See above 2:18.
one who slaughters a wild animal or bird and covers their blood. It is a positive commandment to cover with earth the blood of the slaughter of a wild animal and a bird (see Hilchot Shechitah 14:1).
until the evening. The end of the festival.

a creature that is in doubt whether it is a wild animal or a domestic animal. An animal about which there is doubt whether to define it as a wild animal, which is obligated in covering the blood, or a domestic animal, which is exempt from covering, and its blood must be covered out of doubt (see ibid. 14:4).

lest the one who sees say it is definitely a wild animal... and come to permit its fat. For if they cover its blood on a festival, an observer might think this animal is a definite wild animal, and come to permit its fat for eating as the fat of a wild animal. But in truth its fat is forbidden for eating because it is also possibly a domestic animal, whose fat is forbidden (Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot 7:1).

one who slaughters a wild animal or bird from the eve of the festival shall not cover their blood on the festival. For one does not cover the blood on Shabbat and a festival (see Hilchot Shechitah 14:4); only when he slaughtered on the festival itself may he also cover the blood as a continuation of the act of slaughter.

if he slaughtered a domestic animal, wild animal and bird on a festival and their blood got mixed, he may not cover it until the evening. For the mixture contains the blood of a domestic animal, which is not obligated in covering, and this blood may not be covered on a festival.

and if he had prepared earth... and can cover everything with one poke, he may cover it. For in that same action he certainly also covers the blood of the wild animal and bird that are obligated in covering.

it is permitted for him to pluck wool at the place of the knife by hand. Since plucking wool by hand is not the usual way of shearing, it is not considered a complete labor, and they permitted it for the sake of slaughter.

but with a bird he may not pluck, because that is its way and he would be found plucking on a festival. Since with a bird the usual way is to pluck the feathers by hand, it is considered a complete labor (see Hilchot Shabbat 9:7; Commentary to the Mishnah, Bekhorot 3:3), and therefore it was not permitted for the sake of slaughter.
for this is tanning. Salting the hide falls under the labor of tanning, which is one of the primary labors forbidden on Shabbat (see Hilchot Shabbat 11:5).

but he may place it before a place of treading so that they tread on it and it not be ruined. He may put it in a place where people walk, and those who walk tread on it with their feet, so it does not spoil.
and it is permitted to salt meat for roasting on top of the hide. The meat he wants to roast he may salt on top of the flayed hide so that the falling salt scatters on it.

but for a pot it is forbidden to salt on the hide. When salting meat for roasting, the drawing out of blood is done mainly by the roasting and little salt is needed, whereas for making meat kosher for cooking much salt is needed (see Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot 6:10-12), and such salting is forbidden on the hide.
and likewise one does not salt the fats, etc.. These actions are done so that the fats do not spoil.

one who removes all the meat through one leg so that the whole hide comes out whole and is not torn. The one who removes the meat takes out all the meat of the animal through one hole in the hide that he makes in one of the legs, so that the hide remains whole and can be used as a container for water and the like.
and likewise it is forbidden to make a handle in the meat. It is forbidden to make a cut in the meat that creates a place to hold.
provided he does it with a knife. But if he does it with his hand, it is permitted.

and it is permitted to make a mark in the meat. It is permitted to cut the meat with a knife in a certain way so as to have a mark on it and be able to identify it (and see Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot 8:12).

they scald the head and the feet and singe them in fire, etc.. It is permitted to pour boiling water on the head and feet of an animal or to singe them in fire to remove the hair from them, but one may not smear clay or earth on them for this purpose.
with his shears. With his special scissors.
but one may prepare food that has thorns. That grows with its thorns, since with these foods there is great effort in removing them by hand (R. Y. Kafih).
artichoke. Artichoke. [Note: This is the reading in some manuscripts and printings, and also in the Commentary to the Mishnah, Kil'ayim 5:8; some manuscripts have kronos.]
and akkavit. A species close to the artichoke.
it is permitted to knead a large dough on a festival. Even though he does not need all of the bread for the festival.

and one who kneaded dough from the eve of the festival does not separate challah from it on a festival. For it is forbidden to separate challah on Shabbat and a festival, just as one does not separate terumot and tithes (see Hilchot Shabbat 23:9).
and if he kneaded it on the festival he separates challah from it. Since this is part of preparing the bread and falls under the permission for food preparation.
for burning impure consecrated items is a positive commandment. Hilchot Pesulei ha-Mukdashin 19:1.
in a new furnace. A large new oven made of earthenware that has not yet hardened, and there is concern that it will break and spoil the bread.
one does not rake out an oven or a stove, but one may flatten the ashes in them. It is forbidden to clear out the ashes that accumulate in the oven, but only to level them by hand.
and one seals the mouth of the oven. The crack between the oven and its cover, so that its heat is retained.

provided he softened it the night before, but to knead clay on a festival is forbidden. Clay may be used only if it was prepared from the eve of the festival and does not need water added to soften it, but it is forbidden to add water to it on a festival to soften it.
and it is permitted to knead ashes. For there is no kneading with ashes (Hilchot Shabbat 8:16).

a new oven and stove are not smeared with oil... to harden them. These actions, whose purpose is to strengthen the oven, are forbidden on a festival because it is forbidden to repair a vessel on a festival.
rub. Scrub.
and if in order to bake in them. If he wants to cool the oven so that it will not be too hot.

and one may bake in a large oven and heat water in an antichi. It is permitted to bake in a large oven and to boil water in an antichi, a large water heater in which the fire is in the lower chamber and the water in the upper part.

one does not make cheese on a festival, for if he curdled it from the eve of the festival there is no loss of taste. Curdling cheese is a forbidden labor (see Hilchot Shabbat 7:6), and it was not permitted even for the sake of food preparation because its taste is not impaired if it is prepared before the festival (see above 1:7-8).
groats. Wheat kernels that are divided into several parts by crushing.
one does not sift it a second time on a festival. One does not sift it again to make it cleaner.
and if he changed, it is permitted. To sift it a second time.

for example, that he sift from the back of the sieve or that he sift on the table. He turned the sieve over and sifted on its other side, or sifted over a table and not over a bowl made for that purpose.

one may rub ears of grain and crumble legumes. It is permitted to rub the ears between his fingers to separate the grain kernels from them, and to crumble the pods to take the legumes out of them (compare Hilchot Shabbat 21:14).
and he may blow by hand by hand with all his strength and eat. He may sort a little of the mixture each time by blowing with his mouth to blow away the husks.
and even with a kanon or a tamchui. He may sort even with the help of a tray or bowl (unlike Shabbat, on which they decreed against this manner; see ibid. 21:17).
but not with a sieve, a tablet or a colander. For with these vessels the way is to sort a large amount of food.
when does this apply. When he removes the waste from the food.

when the food is more than the waste. For then it is easier to sort by taking the waste out of the food, since the sorting permitted on a festival is where he reduces the effort (unlike Shabbat, on which the permitted sorting is only in a way that takes the food out of the waste, and only on condition that he sorts by hand and for immediate eating; see Hilchot Shabbat 8:12).
and if there was effort in sorting the waste from the food, etc.. For example, the waste is fine and hard to grasp and remove.
one does not strain mustard. In order to separate its coarse and fine parts.
because it looks like sorting. Although he is not really sorting food from waste, since the coarse part is also fit for eating.

but one may put an egg in a mustard strainer and it strains by itself. It is permitted to put a raw egg in the strainer and the mustard strains on its own with the help of the egg, in which case the straining is done incidentally (see also Hilchot Shabbat 8:14).
strainer. A strainer in which they strain the remains of wine that remains mixed with the lees.
but he should not hang it at the start, so as not to do it as he does on a weekday. Compare ibid. 21:17.

and likewise very sharp naphtha, which is like water, that they shake until it ignites. A highly refined substance obtained from petroleum which is extremely volatile. Because of its great volatility and low flash point, shaking such a liquid and its heating as a result can cause it to ignite.
or a clear hard vessel... which one places opposite the eye of the sun until its brightness returns to flax. Actions similar to igniting with a magnifying glass.

but to produce fire is forbidden, for it is possible to produce it from the evening. Although by the strict law it is permitted to kindle fire on a festival, even not for the sake of eating, the Sages forbade it, just as they forbade labors for the sake of eating that could be done from the eve of the festival (see above 1:4-5).

one does not raise the mouth of the lamp upward so that it goes out. It is forbidden to tilt the lamp in a way that raises the side where the wick is threaded, so that the oil flows to the lower side and away from the wick, and the flame goes out sooner than it should have.
and one does not remove the oil from it. It is forbidden to take oil out of the lamp, for this hastens the extinguishing (see also Hilchot Shabbat 12:2).
and he does not cut the head of the wick with a tool. To remove the charred end.
shakes off. Shakes and removes.

and it is not like removing oil from a lamp. Since the oil is a single unit that burns and removing oil hastens the extinguishing of the flame, whereas in a bundle of wood each piece stands by itself.
just as one does not extinguish on Shabbat. Hilchot Shabbat 12:3.

and one does not extinguish the lamp because of marital relations. For it is forbidden to have marital relations by lamplight (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 21:10), and they did not permit extinguishing on a festival for this purpose.
to another house. To another room.
lest he come to use something attached on a festival. And it is forbidden to use a tree on Shabbat and a festival (see Hilchot Shabbat 21:6).
because it extinguishes. For placing the incense on the coals extinguishes them somewhat.
even to smell it. And it is not considered a bodily need that was permitted under food preparation (see above 1:16).
to perfume the house and the vessels. To put incense on coals to spread a pleasant scent in the house or in the vessels.
and one sweetens mustard with a metal coal. By placing a coal in it.
but not with a wooden coal. Because it extinguishes (but one who extinguishes a metal coal is exempt; Hilchot Shabbat 12:2).
one does not blow with a bellows. To fan the fire.
and one does not twist the wick. It is forbidden to twist it.
and one does not singe it. It is forbidden to singe a wick to make it easy to light.
presses it by hand. To shape the form of the wick.
and soaks it in oil. So that it will light well.
and one places it between two lamps. He puts the ends of the wick in the mouths of two lamps.
the paper. Hard paper on which they used to roast.
they break open. Break.
salted. Salted meat.
that became warped. That became bent.
that are joined at the start of their making. That were made in pairs.
one does not reduce them to two. One does not break the joining point to separate them.
to see a knife for an ignoramus. For a sage to check the blade of a knife to see if it is fit for slaughter (see Hilchot Shechitah 1:26).
with an axe. A hatchet.
with a saw. A kind of saw.
with a butcher's knife. A tool for cutting meat.
for it was possible for him to split from the eve of the festival. And the Sages forbade doing on a festival a labor that could be done from the eve of the festival (above 1:5).
for he might encounter a thick piece of wood and be unable to kindle it. For the wood that comes to hand might be too thick to use as it is without splitting into small pieces.

a brand to roast with. A piece of wood to serve as a spit (and although it is permitted to move wood for cooking, here it is forbidden because he moves the other pieces of wood that he does not need; Mirkevet ha-Mishneh).
in a split of a beam. A piece of wood cut from a beam.
for they did not permit moving wood on a festival except for heating alone. Because of food preparation, as above 1:17.
one removes shop shutters. A kind of removable doors with which shops are locked.
if they have a hinge in the middle. In the middle of the door, in which case the weight does not rest on the hinge.

but if they have a hinge at the side it is forbidden, as a decree lest he drive it in. Since the weight of the door is on the hinge, there is concern that because of this he will press it in when he returns it, and that is forbidden as the labor of building (Hilchot Shabbat 10:13).

vessels that are in sections... one may set them up on a festival, provided that he does not drive them in. Vessels made of several parts may be assembled, but one may not join the parts tightly, because that resembles building.

because there is no building in vessels. In vessels that are normally assembled and taken apart there is no Torah prohibition of building even if he drives them in (see Hilchot Shabbat 22:26), and for this reason they did not decree and forbid assembling them because of the concern that he might come to drive them in.

the stones of the toilet may be turned aside, etc.. They permitted arranging the stones of the toilet for sitting. Although this involves temporary building, which is forbidden by the Sages, in this case it was permitted out of respect for human dignity.
and likewise the bed, he holds the boards upward and inserts the legs beneath them. And see Hilchot Shabbat 22:28.
even though they make a wound. Although a wound may form from removing them, it is permitted since he does not intend it (Commentary to the Mishnah, Beitzah 2:7).
and blows into its nose. To clear the mucus blocking the airways.
and puts a teat into its mouth. So that it will nurse.
a lump of salt. A block of salt.
so that she will have mercy on it. That through these actions she will smell its scent and remember the pain of birth and have mercy on it.
but for an impure animal it is forbidden to do so, because it is not needed. For with an impure animal these actions are of no use (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 128b).

a vessel that was pure for terumah and he wants to immerse it for sacred offerings is permitted to immerse it, etc.. It is permitted to immerse with an immersion that does not purify from impurity but adds purity, such as a vessel that was immersed for terumah and he wants to immerse it for sacred offerings. By Torah law the vessel is pure, and all these immersions are due to stringencies that the Sages made regarding immersion (Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tum'ah 13:2).

a decree lest he leave it in its impurity. And rely on being able to immerse it on the festival, and it would look as if he is preparing his work on the festival (Meiri, Beitzah 18a, and compare Hilchot Shabbat 23:8).

and if he needed to immerse the water in it, he immerses the vessel in its water and is not concerned. If the water in it is also impure, he may immerse the vessel along with the water and there is no concern of prohibition.
a vessel that became impure on a festival may be immersed on a festival. For they decreed only if he could have immersed it on the eve of the festival, as explained above.
if the vessel became impure through impure liquids that are offspring of impurity. Whose impurity is light, and the Sages decreed that such liquids defile vessels.
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tum'ah 7:2.
and one draws with an impure bucket and it becomes pure by itself. It is permitted to draw water from a pit or well with an impure bucket and it becomes purified incidentally.

a niddah who has no clothes to change into acts cunningly and immerses in her clothes. If she has no other garment to wear after she is purified, she is permitted to act cunningly and immerse with impure clothes in order to purify them as well through her immersion (and a person may immerse to purify himself on Shabbat and a festival; see Hilchot Shabbat 23:8).
the decree concerning buying and selling. The Sages' decree not to borrow and lend, buy and sell, hire and rent on Shabbat, lest he write (Hilchot Shabbat 23:12).
one does not set prices. One does not fix the price of the animal.
and they divide among themselves. The partners in the purchase divide the animal.
and when they divide among themselves. On a festival.
when they divide. The meat.
for one does not pay attention to the pan of a scale at all. It is forbidden to use scales in any way, even not for weighing.
even to put meat in it to guard it from mice. When the scales are hung up and raised in the air.
it is forbidden if the scales are hanging. Because in this way placing something in them looks like an act of weighing.
and an expert butcher. Whose hand is skilled in weighing.
and it is forbidden to weigh with a vessel full of water. By placing the meat in a vessel with water one can know the amount of meat.

and one does not cast lots on the portions. It is forbidden to cast lots over portions of meat intended for diners. Casting chalashim is a lottery using various objects, each of which represents a different one of the diners, and another person who does not know which belongs to whom places each object on a particular portion, and thus the lottery is decided (Commentary to the Mishnah, Shabbat 23:2).

but one may cast lots on the meat of sacred offerings on a festival in order to make the commandment beloved. For striving to eat and receive a large portion of the meat of sacred offerings is a commandment (Commentary to the Mishnah, Shabbat 23:2, and see Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 10:1).
to the butcher. A butcher who sells meat.
but give me a portion. The animal is divided into known portions and thus one can buy without mentioning a monetary price.

and likewise he should not take from the shopkeeper by measure or by weight. Buying from a shopkeeper has the same law as buying meat from the butcher, and is likewise permitted on condition that he does not state explicitly a volume or weight.
so that he not spoil his dish. For if he gives more or less than proper he might spoil the dish.
any price. A monetary price.
a total count. Summing up and calculating how what he took now adds to the other debts he has, as he explains.
rather he takes without specifying. And states only the amount he took now.
fattener. A person who fattens animals.
his regular supplier. From whom he is accustomed to buy.
a festival loan. For example, where he took from the butcher or the shopkeeper on a festival in order to repay him after the holiday, as mentioned in the previous halakhot.
they sue for it in court. It is permitted to sue for it in court, and there is no concern that the permission to sue will cause the lender to write a document of proof of the debt on the festival.
although one does not separate terumah and tithes on a festival as on Shabbat. Because it looks like repairing (Hilchot Shabbat 23:9; and see further ibid. 23:14).

and needless to say challah, the foreleg, cheeks and maw, which he takes to the priest on a festival. For it is even permitted to separate them on a festival (see above 3:8; and Commentary to the Mishnah, Beitzah 1:6).
and charity collectors. Who collect food each day for the poor (Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 9:2).
and they distribute to each neighborhood by itself. And not in a central distribution.
although carrying out was permitted on a festival even not for need. As above 1:4-6.
he should not hang the basket behind him. He should not put it on his back.
and one does not go out in a chair, with one behind a man or behind a woman. One does not carry a person sitting in a chair while another person pushes it from behind (Yad Peshutah).
in an apiryon. A chair made for carrying people.
although wherever the Sages forbade because of appearances, etc.. See Hilchot Shabbat 22:20.
on roofs of equal height. In their height.
and he should not lower them by a rope from the windows. He should not lower fruit from the roof with a rope.
but he may slide them, even through a skylight, from place to place on the same roof. He may move them to another place on the same roof, in order to lower them down through the skylight.
that are used. That are made use of.
such as tefillin. For one does not put on tefillin on a festival (Hilchot Tefillin 4:10).

one who makes an eruv techumin for a festival, his animals, vessels and fruit are like him. On a festival, as on Shabbat, it is forbidden to go outside the two-thousand-cubit boundary around the city unless a person fixed his rest in another place by means of an eruv techumin, in which case he may walk two thousand cubits from the place of his eruv (see Hilchot Shabbat 27:1, Hilchot Eruvin 6:1, 8:4). On a festival, when carrying is permitted, it is permitted to take the animal and the vessels anywhere that the owners themselves are permitted to go.
they are like the feet of the one who acquired them. He may carry them as far as he can walk on foot, for since he acquired them, their law is that of his belongings.
and a gentile's belongings acquire rest in their place. And it is forbidden to carry them more than two thousand cubits from the place where they were at the entrance of the festival.

fruit that went outside their boundary, etc.. Since fruit has no will of its own, its law is that of a person who went out and returned under duress, who is as if he did not go out (see Hilchot Shabbat 27:12).
one who hands over his animal to his son, it is like the father's feet. For with his son too it is considered to be in the father's possession.

and even if he gave it to him on a festival, it is like the shepherd's feet. Although the giving actually took place on the festival, since from the eve of the festival he had intended to give it to the shepherd, it is like his feet (see below halakhah 15).

if he handed it over to two shepherds, it is like its owners' feet, because neither of them acquired it. Since it is not entirely in the possession of either of them, it remains like the owner's feet.
another acquired for them. The host of the meal gave them their share in the meal by means of another person (see Hilchot Eruvin 1:20).
and likewise one whose fruit was deposited in another city. And it is outside his walking boundary and he cannot go there.
if he designated for them a corner. He set aside a special place for them, in which case the fruit is still considered in the possession of the depositor.
a pit of an individual. A private water pit.
and those of the returnees from Babylonia which are given over to all. That are meant for the use of pilgrims.
flowing rivers and gushing springs are like the feet of every person. Since the water flows constantly, they do not acquire rest at all.
an ox of the pasture. An ox grazing in a common pasture of the townspeople (Yad Peshutah).
and an ox of fattening. A fattened ox.
although each one took his portion, all the meat is like the feet of both. Since on the eve of the festival the animal was in the partnership of both.

since boundaries are rabbinic there is bererah in them, etc.. Bererah means treating an uncertain situation that will become clear in the future as though it is already clear now. In the case of the barrel, although the division was done on the festival itself, the portion that came to each one is treated as though it had been his already from the eve of the festival, and it is like his feet. The rule is that in Torah law there is no bererah, and in rabbinic law there is bererah (see also Hilchot Eruvin 8:7, Hilchot Terumot 1:21).

and this prohibition is rabbinic, etc.. By Torah law it is permitted to cook on a festival for Shabbat, and the Sages forbade cooking for the sake of an adjacent Shabbat so that he not come to cook for a weekday (see above 1:9).
therefore, etc.. Since the prohibition is rabbinic
,. they permitted it by means of an eruv tavshilin.
and why is it called an eruv. For unlike eruvei chatzerot, in which the food joins the residents of the courtyard together (Hilchot Eruvin 1:6), here the food does not join anything.

for just as the eruv made in courtyards and alleys on Friday is because of a reminder, etc.. For by strict law all of them fall under the category of a private domain and it is permitted to carry in them (see ibid. 1:1-4).
from domain to domain. From a private domain to a public domain, or the reverse, which are forbidden by the Torah.
whether for one or for thousands. An eruv with an olive's bulk serves as an eruv for an unlimited number of people.
with groats. Crushed wheat for making porridge.
relish. Food eaten together with bread.

shaluk. Lightly cooked in water without spices (note of R. Y. Kafih to the Commentary to the Mishnah, Berakhot 6:8; and see Commentary to the Mishnah, Terumot 10:11, Hilchot Nedarim 9:1). Some explain that shaluk means well cooked (Rashi, Nedarim 49a and elsewhere; and see Meiri there, that the word is explained in both senses, all depending on context).
and rinsing them is their cooking for eating. See also Hilchot Shabbat 9:2.
to acquire for them. To grant them a share in the eruv.

as he acquires with eruvei Shabbat, etc.. Similar to eruvei chatzerot and techumin, where he grants them to others through another person who performs an act of acquisition in the eruv for them, and thus they have a share in the eruv (for details see Hilchot Eruvin 1:20; and see also ibid. 6:19).

and he need not inform those for whom he acquired from the eve of the festival, etc.. Since eruv tavshilin is a benefit and the rule is that one may confer a benefit on a person in his absence (see Hilchot Eruvin 1:20), even if they learn of it on the festival itself they may rely on the eruv.
is obligated to bless. The blessing for the commandment, although it is a rabbinic commandment (see Hilchot Berakhot 11:3).
and it is forbidden to another who set one aside for himself. An eruv tavshilin.
until he transfers it to him. That the one who did not set one aside transfers his flour to the one who did.
and if he acted cunningly. That he cooked ostensibly for the festival but intended to prepare for Shabbat (see also above 1:11).

everyone would act cunningly and the name of eruv tavshilin would be forgotten. For if everyone acted cunningly and cooked without an eruv, the commandment of the eruv would be forgotten and they would think one may cook for Shabbat without an eruv.

two festival days, etc.. In the Diaspora they would observe two festival days out of doubt as to which of them is the correct day (see Hilchot Kiddush ha-Chodesh 5:4; and see further below halakhah 14). Since only one of them is holy, he may place an eruv on the first festival day and stipulate that if the first day is the holy one, the second is a weekday and he may cook on it for Shabbat without the eruv; and if the first is a weekday, he is making the eruv now as on any eve of a festival, and the next day, on the real festival, he cooks for Shabbat on the strength of the eruv.

two baskets of tevel. Two baskets of fruit from which terumot and tithes had not been separated. And although it is forbidden to separate terumot and tithes on a festival (above 4:26), he may eat the fruit on the second festival day by separating conditionally.
let this be terumah for that. Let the separation I make on the fruit in one basket also take effect for the other basket (see Hilchot Ma'aser 7:11).

and he designates it by name and sets it aside. He separates by speech and designates its fruit as terumah, and he does not eat from it that day, lest today be a festival and according to his condition he has not yet separated.
and the next day, on the second, he again says. Over the same basket.
and he eats the second. For in any case the terumah was separated on a weekday according to his condition.

but on the two festival days of Rosh Hashanah. For although people observe two days out of doubt, the Sages nevertheless enacted that they are considered one long day, and so one cannot stipulate conditions about them (above 1:24).

14-15. All these things that we said, etc.. At the time when the month was sanctified on the basis of sighting and the Diaspora did not know when the festival fell, they would observe it for two days out of doubt, and then they could place an eruv on the first day and stipulate. But nowadays when the festival is fixed by calculation of the calendar and there is no doubt when the festival falls, the reason the festival is observed for two days is that the Sages instituted continuing the custom they practiced before, of observing two days (Hilchot Kiddush ha-Chodesh 5:4-5; and see above 1:21), and for this reason one cannot stipulate, since both days are holy: the first by Torah law, and the second by rabbinic enactment.
nor eruvei chatzerot nor shittufei mevo'ot. For in them too one could stipulate as with eruv tavshilin (see Hilchot Eruvin 8:14-15).

as it is said, the holy day of the Lord honored. And before that the verse says: "and call the Sabbath a delight," and the text is interpreted here as if delight and honor refer both to Shabbat and to the festivals, which are "the holy day of the Lord."
and we already explained the honor and delight in Hilchot Shabbat. Chapter 30.
and likewise it is proper for a person not to dine on the eves of festivals, etc.. See Hilchot Shabbat 30:4.
as if attached to idolatry. And he has no share in the World to Come (Hilchot Teshuvah 3:14).
and the eight days of the festival. Sukkot and Shemini Atzeret.
all of them are forbidden for eulogy and fasting. See Hilchot Ta'aniyot 1:6, 1:9, Hilchot Evel 11:3.
as we explain in Hilchot Chagigah. 1:1.
included in that rejoicing is to rejoice. The commandment of rejoicing includes not only the festival offering but also his own rejoicing and that of his household.
roasted nuts. Kinds of roasted seeds.
and sweets. Kinds of confections.
and when he eats and drinks, etc.. See also Hilchot Chagigah 2:14.

their sacrifices shall be like the bread of mourners; all who eat it shall be defiled, for their bread is for their own appetite. The meat they eat will be like the food of mourners, which defiles whoever eats it, since they eat it for themselves and do not share with the poor (see also Hilchot Chagigah 2:14, Hilchot Megillah 2:17).

and such rejoicing is a disgrace to them, as it is said, and I will spread dung on your faces, the dung of your festivals. God will scatter in their faces the dung of the sacrifice that they eat only for themselves (see also Hilchot De'ot 5:1).
such is the religion. This is the proper order.
and they are called mo'ed. The intermediate days of a festival are also called "mo'ed" by the Sages (see Commentary to the Mishnah, Mo'ed Katan 1:1).
and they are forbidden for eulogy and fasting. See Hilchot Ta'aniyot 1:7, 1:9, Hilchot Evel 11:3.
a Torah scholar in his presence. Before he is buried.
and needless to say on Rosh Chodesh, Chanukah and Purim. For on them there is no obligation of rejoicing by Torah law, as there is on the intermediate days (as above halakhah 16).
one does not set... and one does not mourn on the festival. See also Hilchot Evel 11:3.
but from his house to his grave. They take the dead person from his house straight to burial.
and likewise one does not tear, etc.. See also ibid. 11:1-2.
and if he was a sage or a worthy person. The deceased.
or who was standing at the time of the departure of the soul. One who was present at the time of death (see ibid. 9:11).
women on the intermediate days. See also Hilchot Evel 11:4-5.
responding. Reciting a dirge together.
clapping. Striking hand against hand, or on the thigh, the face or the heart.
lamenting. One recites a dirge and all respond to her.
that he stir up weeping over his dead. To arouse weeping for the dead person.
thirty days before the festival. This is speaking of one who died before then; but if he died within these thirty days, one may stir up weeping for him (see ibid. 11:6).

since it is called a holy convocation. The Sages interpreted the verse that summarizes the passage on the festivals: "These are the appointed times of the Lord, which you shall proclaim as holy convocations, to bring a fire offering to the Lord..." (Leviticus 23:37) as referring to the intermediate days, on which special offerings are brought during the festivals (see a memorial to the festival offering, Chagigah 18a), and from this the intermediate days are called a "holy convocation" and work is forbidden on them.
and it is the time of the festival offering in the Temple. For one who did not bring the festival offering on the first day brings it on the intermediate days (see Hilchot Chagigah 1:4-5).
rabbinic lashes. Lashes by rabbinic law.
for the end of the matter is in the things forbidden on it, etc.. The purpose of the prohibition of work on the intermediate days is that it should not be entirely like a weekday.
an irrigated field. A field watered with water, which does not need further irrigation to save it from great loss.
beit ha-shelahin, which is the thirsty land. For "meshalhe" is the Aramaic for tired (that is, thirsty).
he may not draw and water. He may not draw with a bucket and water the field.

whether it first emerged. Even if the spring's channel is new and its sides are not stable, and there is no concern that they will collapse and he will have to labor to repair them during the festival.
he draws it and waters with it. He directs the spring to flow and water the field.

a person may turn his olives on the intermediate days. Before producing oil they place the olives in a pile to soften them, and one must turn them from time to time so they do not spoil from the heat generated in the pile.
and grinds them. Places them under the beam of the olive press so that the oil comes out under pressure.
and treads them. Presses them again to extract the remaining oil in the olives.
and fills the barrels. With oil.
and seals them. Plugs the opening of the barrel.
and takes his flax out of the steeping so that it not be lost. Takes out the raw flax that he put in soaking water so that it does not rot in it.
and likewise a vineyard whose time to be harvested arrives during the intermediate days, they harvest it. Since the grapes would spoil if they are not harvested in time.
skilled. An expert.
stitches in alternation. Sews intermittently and not with continuous stitching (Commentary to the Mishnah, Mo'ed Katan 1:8, according to the opinion of R. Yochanan in the Gemara).
and in building. See below 8:6 for what is permitted to build during the intermediate days.
and smooths the cracks of the ground. Rubs cracked places to smooth the surface of the ground.
and rolls them by hand and foot, as they roll in the cloth-fulling. He may smooth them by hand and foot, similar to what he normally does with vessels.
and likewise anything similar. For anything he needs during the festival it is permitted to do even if there is no loss, provided that he does it with a change.
pickled foods. Preserved foods.

for it is possible that he will eat from them during the festival. Although heavily salted fish are not fit for eating until the saltiness is soaked out, since he can remove the saltiness by squeezing and pressing and eat them thus during the festival, it is permitted to salt them.
one may put in beer. It is permitted to put fruit into water so that it ferments and beer is made from it.
for this cunning is not noticeable to the observer. For the observer does not know that he has old beer at home.
damage to the waters. What was destroyed and damaged in the water channels.
ditches. Elongated pits.
and caves. Covered pits.
and they measure the mikvaot. To check whether they contain forty se'ah, which is the measure of a mikveh valid for immersion.
they draw water to it. They bring water to it.
to declare ownerless the mixed kinds. The court's agents would declare ownerless fields whose owners grew mixed kinds in them (see Hilchot Kil'ayim 2:15-17).
valuations. One who vowed to give a person's valuation gives his fixed valuation to the Temple treasury (see Hilchot Arachin va-Charamim 1:1-3).
devoted things. One who vowed to Heaven using the language of cherem may redeem the thing he vowed for money (see ibid. 6:4).
consecrated things. One who consecrated an animal or object to the Temple may redeem them for their value.
and they give the suspected adulteresses to drink. A married woman suspected of adultery must drink the bitter waters in order to be permitted to her husband (see Hilchot Sotah 1:2).
and they burn the heifer. The red heifer, whose ashes are used for purification.

and they break the neck of the heifer. The eglah arufah, used to atone for the people of the place for a slain person who was found and it is not known who killed him (see Hilchot Rotze'ach, chapters 9-10).
and they pierce a Hebrew slave. They pierce the ear of a Hebrew slave who wishes to remain a slave after six years of service (see Hilchot Avadim 3:9).
and they purify the leper. They carry out the purification process of the leper (see Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 4:1-2).
and they mark the graves. ...
so that the priests will keep away from them. They renew the marking that is made on graves so that the priests will not approach them.
and laws of lashes. Laws whose punishment is lashes.
they excommunicate. They place under a ban.
deeds of valuation that they valued for a creditor. Documents describing what they assessed from the debtor's property to collect his debt for the creditor.
and deeds by which they sold for the maintenance of the wife and daughters. A document recording the court's decision to sell from the husband's property for their maintenance.
and bills of halitzah and of mi'un. Documents in which a court attests to a halitzah or mi'un (annulment of a girl's childhood marriage) performed before it.
and betrothals of women. A betrothal document, for one who betroths with a document.
and receipts. Confirmation of receipt of money.
and gifts. A document of giving a gift.
correct. Fix.
in the Torah scroll of the Temple court. The Torah scroll from which they read in the Temple.
and spins techelet (blue wool) for his garment. Spins threads of techelet for his garment that requires tzitzit.
for people are not careful about the proper preparation of the writing of these. That is, he is not as particular about the manner of writing as he is with books, tefillin and mezuzot.
his expenses. His costs.
and if the person was well known, they may even do so in the marketplace. For then everyone knows that the coffin is being prepared for the dead man and not for another purpose.
we do not examine plagues during the festival. A kohen does not examine a mark suspected of being tzara'at (a skin affliction) (and see also Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 9:8).
they may cut hair. Get haircuts.
unkempt. Dirty and disordered.

a mourner whose seventh day fell on a festival. The seventh day of mourning, when he could not do laundry on the eve of the festival because laundering is forbidden during the seven days of mourning (see also Hilchot Evel 10:7).
and one who was under a ban. He is forbidden to cut hair or do laundry until his ban is lifted (see Hilchot Talmud Torah 7:4).
and did not ask a sage and have his vow released. That is, he could have his vow released by a sage (see Hilchot Nedarim 4:5, Hilchot Shevuot chapter 6).

but a nazirite and a metzora... may cut their hair during the festival so as not to delay their offerings. A nazirite and a metzora are commanded to shave their hair before bringing their offerings (see Hilchot Nazir 8:6, Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 11:1).
and anyone who emerges from impurity to purity may cut his hair during the festival. Since it is not fitting for a person to beautify himself while impure (Maggid Mishneh).

and members of a priestly watch whose watch ended during the festival, etc.. Kohanim whose week of service ended during the intermediate days of the festival may cut their hair, since during their week of service they are forbidden to cut it (see also Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 1:12-13).
to trim the mustache. To cut the mustache.
and to cut the nails. To clip them.
and removing hair. Taking it off.
her cosmetics. Various beauty treatments, which are explained below.
applying eye makeup. Putting kohl on her eyes.
and braiding. Plaiting her hair.
rouge. A red dye.
and she plasters herself with lime and the like. She puts lime or another substance on her body, to warm and redden the skin or to remove hair.
provided she can peel it off during the festival. For then she enjoys the treatment during the festival and does not merely suffer from it.
hand towels. Towels for the hands.
and Torah scroll wrappers. Cloths in which Torah scrolls are wrapped and which are held during the reading (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kilayim 9:3).
and bath towels. A towel for the whole body.
linen garments. Garments of flax, which get dirty quickly and need to be laundered again even if they were washed before the festival.
opens onto a corner. A street corner.
or onto an alley. A street that branches off from the public domain.
opens one. One door.

and on the eve of the last festival day of Sukkot he brings out and decorates the marketplace with fruit in honor of the festival. Since the last festival day of Sukkot (Shemini Atzeret) is a festival in its own right and has extra joy.
spice sellers may sell in their usual way, openly. Since it is clear that they are selling for the needs of the festival.
what will he eat. What he will eat, as above 7:13.
one may hire a worker during the festival for work to be done after the festival. It is permitted during the intermediate days to agree with a worker that he will do work for him after the festival.
and a gentile who took on a contract from a Jew. A gentile who does work as a contractor for a Jew and is not his employee; his choice to work during the festival is made on his own initiative.

even if he was outside the Sabbath boundary, he may not let him work during the festival. Unlike the Sabbath, where work beyond the boundary is permitted because on the Sabbath Jews are not likely to be there and there is no concern of suspicion (see Hilchot Shabbat 6:14).
rivers drawn from marshes. Small streams drawn from pools of water.
one may water a irrigated field from them during the festival. For the field would be ruined if it were not watered, as above 7:2.
provided they have not been cut off. That is, the stream is still connected to the marsh, and there is no concern that its water will diminish and he will draw water from it with a vessel.
and likewise ponds between which an aqueduct passes. An aqueduct drawn from a spring that passes between pools of water.
one may water from them. Since even if the ponds dry up, he can water from the aqueduct by flow and will not come to draw from the ponds with a vessel.

and likewise a pond that overflowed from an irrigated field and is still overflowing, etc.. A field irrigated by flow from a spring, some of whose water drips from it into a pond; he may channel water from that pond to a lower irrigated field, provided the upper one continues to be watered from the spring.
half of which is low and half high. And therefore the water that is drawn does not reach the high part.
and one may draw water to water vegetables so as to eat them during the festival. For the needs of the festival, they permitted even extra effort.
basins at the roots of vines. Round hollows around the tree for irrigation.
if it was a handbreadth deep, he may dig it up to six. If he dug only a handbreadth deep, he may dig another five handbreadths.
and one may channel water from tree to tree, provided he does not water the whole field. In a field with trees, he may channel water to the trees but not to the rest of the field.
and if the field was moist, one may water all of it. The whole tree field, since the watering is not noticeable in it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mo'ed Katan 1:3).
and one may moisten the field. Wet it so that it is ready for sowing.
for none of these things involve extra effort. And they were not forbidden during the festival, as above 7:2.
seeds that had not been watered before the festival. A sown area that has not yet been watered.
he may not water them during the festival. Even if this involves great loss, as above 7:2.
the channel. A watercourse that draws water from the spring or the marsh to the field.
trenches. Long pits.
and caves. Covered pits.
they may clear out. Clean of sand and stones.
and plaster their cracks. Smear the cracks of the pit with clay.
but one may not dig them at the outset. Unlike public pits (above 7:10).
even if he does not need them. During the festival; it is permitted to do so because it involves no great effort.
a soaking pit. A pit for soaking, for example for soaking flax.
destroy. Ruin.
in a tree field. A field in which trees grow.
a white field. A field meant for sowing, which is not harmed by mice.
a spit. A peg or rod.
he pulls it out. He takes it out of the ground.
and its place is found to be a hole. The spit leaves a hole in which to hang the trap, so he is not digging the hole in the ordinary manner of digging.
a garden wall that fell down, he may rebuild it in an amateur manner. He places stones one on top of another without plaster (above 7:5).
or fence it off. He closes up the breach.
with reeds and rushes. Plants that grow in standing water and are suitable for various uses.
but a courtyard wall that fell down, he may rebuild it in his usual way. Even as skilled work, since out of concern for theft or loss he builds in his usual manner without change (as above 7:3).
leaning. Tilting.
because of the danger. Lest it collapse and hurt someone.
a bench. A bench.
to sit or sleep on. Since this is included in the needs of the festival.
the pivot. Of the door.
and the socket. A gutter (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mo'ed Katan 1:10). Some explain it as the hole into which the pivot enters (Rashi and others).
and the beam. That holds the door or serves as its bar.
and we have already explained. Above 7:3.
and one may not build it. A grave built above the ground.
ready. Prepared.
one may not remove the dead, etc.. See also Hilchot Evel 11:3 (regarding the festival); there 14:15 (regarding removal in general).
kushut. A parasitic plant used to make beer.
one may not treat trees for worms. Actions to prevent worm damage to the tree.
and one may not smear saplings. Smearing a foul-smelling substance so that creeping creatures keep away from the tree.
and one may not prune. Cutting off branches to improve growth.
but one may anoint trees. It is permitted to anoint with oil a tree that was pruned, so that it does not die.
and the fruit on them. To hasten their ripening.
and one may uproot flax. From the field.
because it is fit to cover things with. For he can use it to cover things.
one may not bring the flock into the pen to fertilize the ground, etc.. Penning a field is moving the pen from place to place in the field so that the animals fertilize it.
and if they came on their own. Gentile shepherds who came with their animals.
to shoo their flock. To move the animals from place to place in the field.
if he was hired by the week, by the month, by the year, or by the septennium. If he hired a gentile for a fixed period and not just for the festival.
the manure in the courtyard. Of the animals.
they move it to the sides. But they do not take it out of the courtyard.
and if the courtyard became like a cattle shed. That is, it filled with manure as is common in a cattle shed.
the one who levels. Smooths.
a heap. A pile.
the one who gathers. Picks, trims.
the one who opens. Opens a water channel to the field.
branches. Branches.
an oven and stove that can dry. That have time to dry and be fit for use (since their ovens were made of clay).
and in either case, one may build on the shard of an oven and on its attached stove. If there is already a clay frame, it is permitted to add plaster to it.
and one may weave the beds. Stretching ropes from side to side of the bed so that a mattress can be placed on it.
and one may chisel millstones. Level and dress them so that they are fit for use.
and open an eye for them. Make a hole in them for feeding grain through the hole between the two stones, or a hole in the side of the upper stone for inserting a pole with which to turn it.
and set them up. In their place.
and one may build the aqueduct of a mill. So that the water flowing through it will turn the millstones.
one may pitch the jar. To seal it.
because it involves no effort. Since it is small, even though there is no great loss.
and one may seal the mouth of a jar of beer. With a stopper.
and one may cover the dried figs. Cover figs spread out to dry.
and one may soften garments by hand. By rubbing.
but one may not make sleeve knots. Tying the folds of the sleeve in a special way for decoration.
a millstone donkey. A donkey that turns the millstones, which is needed for the festival.
but one may bleed it. For healing.
and all foods... for healing, a person may eat and drink during the festival. Even though they are forbidden on the Sabbath (see Hilchot Shabbat 21:20-21).
one may not move. Vessels.
from courtyard to courtyard. From a house in this courtyard to a house in another courtyard.
not from an ugly one to a nice one. Not from an ugly courtyard to a nice courtyard, even though he would be happy to move to a nicer courtyard.
the metalworker. An iron craftsman.
and if the craftsman has nothing to eat. And he needs to be paid and the purchase must be completed during the festival.
and if he does not trust him. He does not rely on the craftsman.
from minchah onward. Toward evening, about two and a half hours before sunset (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 10:1).
like Sabbath eves. See Hilchot Shabbat 5:18-20.
and they stop him. From work.
except for the eve of Pesach after midday. For on the eve of Pesach they were stricter and forbade work from midday, and were also strict in other matters as detailed below.
except for the eve of Pesach... they excommunicate him. See also Hilchot Talmud Torah 6:14.
because it involves a festival offering and the slaughter of a sacrifice. And for this reason it resembles the intermediate days of a festival, as explained in the next halachah (and see above 7:1).
for it is the time of slaughter. Of the Pesach offering (Hilchot Korban Pesach 1:4).
at the outset. The initial start of the work.

he should not appear before them to be idle because of the prohibition. He should not refrain from work in a way that looks to them as though he refrains because it is forbidden, but rather because he has no work to do.
a person should never deviate because of dispute. He should not behave differently from the custom of the place where he is.

and one may set hens on eggs. Arranging the eggs so that a hen will sit on them to warm them (Meiri, Pesachim 55a). Others explain that one puts eggs under a hen and sets up a dovecote structure (Rashi there).
and during the festival. The intermediate days of the festival.
